subject: VAL
label: Grade 08
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 08 Values and life skills, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 4 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Ethical decision making
modules.outcome: weigh choices using a simple framework
modules.intro: In this unit, 'Ethical decision making', you learn to weigh choices using a simple framework. You work with notes, a worked line and a self-mark. You see it, say it, then do it alone.
points: Listen and talk: hear a short story, text or example linked to 'Ethical decision making' and say what it means in your own words.
Connect: name one place in your own day where it applies.
Use it: weigh choices using a simple framework. Practise with care and respect, in class and at home.
Reflect: what went well, what was hard, and one thing you will do next time.
modules.example: Solved: Ethical decision steps: facts, who is affected, options, which value each option meets, choose, review later. Method: Model run for 'Ethical decision making'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Weigh choices using a simple framework: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Situation: Waleed finds a tablet in the corridor with a lock screen photo of a younger child and a name label reading 'Hamad G5'. Nobody else is nearby. He wonders whether to keep it, ignore it or return it.

Step 2, Framework: He uses four questions. Who is affected? What are my options? What are the likely results of each? Which option is honest, fair and caring? Writing the answers helps him think clearly instead of reacting.
Step 3, Who and options: Affected people are Hamad, Hamad's family, Waleed and the school. Options are: keep it, leave it where it is, return it to the office, or find Hamad. Four options are listed.

Step 4, Results: Keeping it harms Hamad and is dishonest. Leaving it risks it being lost. Taking it to the office is safe, honest and quick. Finding Hamad directly could work, but the office can check and avoid mix-ups.
Step 5, Decide: Waleed takes the tablet to the front office, says where he found it, and gives the name on the label. The staff contact Hamad's class teacher. The choice is honest, fair and caring.

Step 6, Review: Later Hamad says thank you. Waleed notes the framework slowed him down just enough to choose well. If the choice were harder, such as being asked to keep it secret, he would talk to a trusted adult.

Your turn: You see a friend copy another student's project and hand it in. Use the four questions. Model answer: affected are the owner, friend, teacher and you; options include silence, talking to the friend, telling the teacher; best is asking your friend to fix it, then reporting if not.

modules.title: Peer pressure
modules.outcome: describe ways to respond to peer pressure
modules.intro: In this unit, 'Peer pressure', you learn to describe ways to respond to peer pressure. You work with notes, a worked line and a self-mark. You see it, say it, then do it alone.
points: Listen and talk: hear a short story, text or example linked to 'Peer pressure' and say what it means in your own words.
Connect: name one place in your own day where it applies.
Use it: describe ways to respond to peer pressure. Practise with care and respect, in class and at home.
Reflect: what went well, what was hard, and one thing you will do next time.
modules.example: Solved: A friend says 'skip class'. Steps: stay calm, say no clearly, offer another plan, walk away, tell a trusted adult if it continues. Method: Model run for 'Peer pressure'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Describe ways to respond to peer pressure: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Situation: At lunch, Ismail's group says, 'We are skipping the last lesson, come with us.' Six friends are going. Ismail does not want to skip because there is a test review, yet he fears being called boring.

Step 2, Spot the pressure: He notices three signs: the group is all agreeing, someone is calling him names if he refuses, and the choice is not his own. Peer pressure is when others push you to act against your own values.

Step 3, Options: Ismail can say yes, say no plainly, say no with an alternative, or walk away. He thinks about what he wants and what might happen: missing the review, getting a detention, or losing some friends.

Step 4, Say no with a line: He says calmly, 'No, I am going to class. I'll see you after school for football.' He uses a short, steady voice, keeps his word choice simple, and offers a different shared plan.

Step 5, Handle a push back: A friend says, 'Come on, don't be a baby.' Ismail answers, 'It's my choice,' and walks to class. He repeats the same sentence and does not argue, because arguing gives the pressure more power.

Step 6, Result and support: Two friends later admit they wished they had stayed. Ismail tells his counsellor about it to be safe. Tools for pressure are: say no, give a reason or alternative, leave, find an ally and tell an adult.
Your turn: Friends dare you to post a rude joke about a teacher. Respond. Model answer: say 'No, I'm not posting that', suggest another activity, walk away, and tell an adult if they keep pushing.

modules.title: Service and gratitude
modules.outcome: plan and review a service act
modules.intro: In this unit, 'Service and gratitude', you learn to plan and review a service act. You work with notes, a worked line and a self-mark. You see it, say it, then do it alone.
points: Listen and talk: hear a short story, text or example linked to 'Service and gratitude' and say what it means in your own words.
Connect: name one place in your own day where it applies.
Use it: plan and review a service act. Practise with care and respect, in class and at home.
Reflect: what went well, what was hard, and one thing you will do next time.
modules.example: Solved: Plan a service project: need, goal, three tasks, who and when, and how you will measure it (for example 50 bags collected). Method: Model run for 'Service and gratitude'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Plan and review a service act: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Choose the act: Grade 8 wants to thank the 12 school support staff: cleaners, guards, canteen and bus helpers. Dalal proposes handwritten thank-you notes and a tidy-up of the staff room. Gratitude means noticing and valuing what others do for us.
Step 2, Plan: There are 4 classes with 24 students each, so 96 students. They agree that every student writes 1 note, so that is 96 notes. 96 divided by 12 staff is 8 notes per person.

Step 3, Set roles: Each class picks a lead, collects notes in a box and sorts them into 12 envelopes, 8 notes each. Dalal checks the count: 12 envelopes times 8 notes is 96, matching the number of students.

Step 4, Do the act: On Thursday the leads hand out envelopes. Notes include specific details, like 'Thank you for opening the gate early every morning.' Specific thanks show real attention, unlike a general 'thank you'.

Step 5, Staff room help: Six volunteers wipe tables and recycle papers in 15 minutes after asking permission. They leave without asking for praise. Service is for the other person, not for being seen.

Step 6, Review: Dalal asks the staff and students what went well. A guard says he kept his note. Next time they plan a thank-you for the bus team. Reviewing improves the next act, and honest feelings are better than claiming huge results.

Your turn: Plan a thank-you act for 5 teachers from 30 students. Model answer: each student writes 1 note, 30 divided by 5 is 6 notes per teacher, 5 envelopes of 6, give them on a set day, then review.

modules.title: Digital wellbeing
modules.intro: In this unit, 'Digital wellbeing', you learn to plan balanced screen time. You work with notes, a worked line and a self-mark. You see it, say it, then do it alone.
points: Listen and talk: hear a short story, text or example linked to 'Digital wellbeing' and say what it means in your own words.
Connect: name one place in your own day where it applies.
Use it: plan balanced screen time. Practise with care and respect, in class and at home.
Reflect: what went well, what was hard, and one thing you will do next time.
modules.example: Solved: Calm routine: name the feeling, breathe in for 4 counts and out for 6, talk to someone, do one small helpful thing. Plan screen time: 1 hour, then a 10-minute break. Method: Model run for 'Digital wellbeing'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Plan balanced screen time: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Find your time budget. A week has 7 times 24, which is 168 hours. Sleep at 8 hours a night takes 56 hours and school at 6 hours on 5 days takes 30. That leaves 82 hours for meals, family, study, sport, hobbies and screens.

Step 2, Track current screen use. Check the device's usage report for a week, or tally it in a notebook. Separate learning use from leisure use. Be honest about the total; a plan only works when it starts from real numbers.

Step 3, Set limits. Plan 2 hours of leisure screen time on 5 school days and 3 hours on 2 weekend days. That is 10 plus 6, which is 16 hours. As a share of the week, 16 divided by 168 is about 9.5 percent.

Step 4, Protect sleep and eyes. Stop screens about an hour before bed and keep the phone out of the bedroom overnight. Use the 20-20-20 habit: every 20 minutes look at something 20 feet (about 6 metres) away for 20 seconds.

Step 5, Add balanced alternatives. Plan time for exercise, face-to-face friends, reading and hobbies. Write the weekly plan in a table with days across the top, and review after 2 weeks to see whether it feels realistic.

Step 6, Your turn: plan screen time of 1.5 hours on 5 weekdays and 2.5 hours on 2 weekend days, and find the weekly total. Answer: 1.5 times 5 is 7.5, plus 2.5 times 2 which is 5, so the total is 12.5 hours.

L2: responsibility, courage and care for others and nature.
